screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to make compute choices that reduce cost without hurting performance. We start by clarifying EC2 purchasing options — On‑Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans and Spot — and when each fits typical workloads. You will also learn right‑sizing techniques for EC2 and Lambda, how container resource requests and limits affect packing and billing for ECS and EKS, and why tagging plus lifecycle automation are essential for governance. I’ll give concrete examples you can use today: recognizing steady 24/7 services that suit Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, tuning Lambda memory to reduce duration, and cleaning up unattached volumes to stop unnecessary charges. Throughout, pay attention to three linked practices: monitor usage, choose the right purchase model, and automate lifecycle actions. These three reduce waste most reliably. By the end you’ll have a checklist to evaluate compute architecture decisions and a clear set of next steps to apply in your environment. Consider one workload you manage: which of these approaches would cut the most cost without adding risk?

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

AWS Compute Cost Optimization

Design decisions for purchasing, sizing, monitoring and lifecycle determine your compute bill. Learn the practical patterns that deliver savings without sacrificing reliability.

Purchasing
Choose On‑Demand, RI, Savings Plans or Spot based on predictability.
Right‑Sizing
Match CPU, memory and I/O to real usage to avoid waste.
Governance
Use Cost Explorer, Budgets, tags and lifecycle automation for control.
In this lesson

You will get a practical checklist for purchasing decisions, right‑sizing workflows for EC2 and Lambda, container resource configuration, and governance actions that prevent waste.

Concept map
Purchase Model
On‑Demand, RI, Savings Plans, Spot
Right‑Size
CPU, memory, I/O, Lambda duration
Lines imply workflow: choose model → monitor → right‑size → automate lifecycle
Coming up
Deep dives on purchasing, right‑sizing, containers, and governance, each with examples and common mistakes to avoid.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to select the appropriate EC2 purchasing option for different workload patterns, from bursty test servers to steady 24/7 services. You will also be able to right‑size both EC2 instances and Lambda functions using utilization metrics and recommendations, improving performance and lowering cost. Additionally, you will understand how to configure container resource requests and limits so ECS and EKS schedules efficiently and avoids costly overprovisioning. Finally, you will apply cost management practices — Cost Explorer, Budgets, tagging, and resource lifecycle automation — to monitor, allocate, and remove wasteful resources. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. For example, the ability to map a predictable 24/7 workload to a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan is a concrete milestone; so is creating a budget with an 80 percent alert threshold. These skills make your designs both cost‑aware and operationally sustainable.

screens.title: EC2 Purchasing Options
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 purchasing options determine how you pay for compute and directly affect cost at scale. On‑Demand instances are the most flexible: they let you start and stop instances with no long‑term commitment, but they are the most expensive per hour. Reserved Instances provide significant discounts for predictable, steady workloads when you commit for one or three years. The chapter notes discounts up to about seventy‑five percent for RIs when combined with the right payment options; they are best for services that run continuously and have consistent sizing. Savings Plans achieve similar or better savings with more flexibility: by committing to a sustained hourly spend for one or three years, you receive discounts that apply across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda — making them suitable for dynamic environments where instance types change. Spot Instances are the low‑cost option for fault‑tolerant, interruptible workloads; they can offer very deep discounts but require architectures that handle interruption. A common mistake is leaving predictable, steady workloads on On‑Demand. In practice, analyze historical utilization, then choose RIs or Savings Plans for steady baselines and Spot for flexible, batch or fault‑tolerant tasks. The core takeaway: match predictability to commitment for maximal savings.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › EC2 Purchasing Options
Definition

Purchase models and tradeoffs

Each model trades commitment for price. Use historical usage to choose the right one and avoid paying premium prices for steady workloads.

On‑Demand
Flexible, no commitment, highest hourly cost. Use for short‑lived or unpredictable workloads.
Reserved Instances (RIs)
Commit 1 or 3 years for deep discounts on steady workloads. All Upfront options often provide the largest savings.
Savings Plans
Commit to consistent hourly compute spend for one or three years; discounts apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda.
Spot Instances
Lowest cost for interruptible workloads; suitable for batch, CI, or fault‑tolerant services.
Key Takeaway

Analyze predictability first, then apply the purchase model that pairs commitment with stability to reduce cost.

Concrete example
A database that runs 24/7 with stable usage is a candidate for a 3‑year Reserved Instance or a 3‑year Compute Savings Plan. A nightly batch job that can restart is a candidate for Spot instances. Savings Plans are preferred when you expect instance types to change, because they apply discounts across compute families.
Common mistake
Keeping predictable, long‑running services on On‑Demand by default. This leaves savings on the table and is avoidable with historical usage analysis.
Check your understanding
  1. Name one scenario where Spot is preferable.
  2. Explain why Savings Plans help when instance types change.

screens.title: Reserved Instances vs Savings Plans
screens.narratorSegment: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans both reduce cost for predictable compute, but they differ in flexibility and scope. Reserved Instances tie discounts to a specific instance family, region and tenancy when using Standard RIs; Convertible RIs allow some instance family changes but require compatible choices. The chapter highlights that RIs are ideal when you have stable, continuous workloads that will run on the same instance family for the commitment term. Savings Plans, by contrast, grant discounts based on a committed hourly spend and apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda. This makes Savings Plans especially useful in modern, dynamic environments where workloads may migrate from EC2 to Fargate or change instance families over time. A common decision pattern is to buy Savings Plans for broad baseline spend and use RIs only when you need instance‑level guarantees. Payment options and term length matter too: one‑year versus three‑year commitments and All Upfront payments affect the effective discount. The practical rule: if you need maximum flexibility across compute types, prefer Savings Plans; if you need instance‑specific pricing and you can commit to the same family, RIs may be slightly better in narrow cases.

keyIdea.title: When to choose
keyIdea.text: Use Savings Plans for flexible, cross‑service commitments; use RIs for narrow, long‑lived instance family commitments when needed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › RIs vs Savings Plans
Reserved Instances

Instance‑level commitment

  • Best for continuous, predictable workloads that match instance families.
  • One‑year or three‑year terms; payment options impact discount.
  • Convertible RIs allow some flexibility between families.
Savings Plans

Spend‑based commitment

  • Apply discounts across EC2, Fargate and Lambda for a committed hourly spend.
  • Preferred for modern architectures where compute types change over time.
  • One‑year or three‑year terms with similar payment choices affecting savings.
Example
A fleet with mixed EC2 and Fargate usage benefits from a Savings Plan that covers baseline spend across both services.
Misconception
Thinking RIs always beat Savings Plans. Savings Plans may be better when compute types shift over time.
Takeaway
Combine Savings Plans for baseline flexibility and RIs only when a fixed instance family is guaranteed and yields extra benefit.

screens.title: Right‑Sizing EC2 Instances
screens.narratorSegment: Right‑sizing EC2 is a process, not a one‑time task. Start by collecting utilization metrics: C P U, memory, network input and output and disk input and output. Use CloudWatch to gather a historical view over several weeks or months, because short spikes can mislead decisions. Feed that usage history into AWS Compute Optimizer when available; it analyzes past behavior and recommends instance sizes, families and EBS volume adjustments. After you have recommendations, test changes with a canary or staging environment and monitor latency, error rates and user experience. If performance holds, plan a rollout and consider RIs or Savings Plans to cover the new, lower baseline. Always avoid two mistakes: downsizing purely on average C P U while ignoring spikes that need burst capacity, and changing sizes without validating real‑world performance. To iterate effectively, keep a rollback plan and tag instances with owner and purpose so you can track impact. The goal is to deliver the same or better performance with less billable capacity. Over time this process should be periodic and data‑driven, not reactive. Right‑Sizing EC2 Instances means measure, analyze with compute optimizer, test changes, validate performance, then commit and monitor to prevent regressions.. In practical terms, a practical workflow to identify and correct over‑provisioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Right‑Sizing EC2
Process

Steps to right‑size

1. Measure
Collect CPU, memory, network and disk metrics over weeks.
2. Analyze
Use Compute Optimizer and patterns to recommend instance families and sizes.
3. Test
Run changes in a canary or staging environment and monitor performance.
4. Rollout & Monitor
Gradually apply changes and track SLAs; have rollback plans.
Illustrative example
An application with average CPU of 20% but periodic spikes to 80% should not be downsized solely on the average. Instead, identify whether spikes are brief bursts that can be handled with instance bursting or require sustained capacity. Use Compute Optimizer recommendations and run an A/B test where a smaller instance is used behind a load test to verify latency under peak conditions.
Common mistake
Relying only on CPU averages or a single metric. Always consider memory, I/O, and traffic patterns before resizing.
Key Takeaway

Right‑sizing is iterative: measure, analyze, test, and monitor to reduce cost without harming performance.

screens.title: Right‑Sizing AWS Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda pricing depends on memory allocation and execution duration. Increasing memory increases C P U proportionally in Lambda, so some functions complete faster when given more memory. That faster completion can lower overall billed duration and therefore cost, despite the higher per‑millisecond memory price. Right‑sizing a function is an experiment: measure current Duration and Invocations in CloudWatch, try a higher memory configuration, and compare cost per invocation. The chapter recommends using the Duration metric to find the sweet spot. A concrete example: if a function at 512 MB runs in 300 milliseconds, and at 1024 MB it runs in 120 milliseconds, the second configuration can be cheaper per invocation even though memory doubled. A common misconception is that higher memory always costs more; in Lambda, C P U scaling can reduce duration enough to lower cost. The practical workflow is to test multiple memory sizes, record Duration and cost, and choose the memory setting that minimizes cost while meeting latency requirements. Right‑Sizing AWS Lambda means test memory sizes because more memory increases cpu and can reduce duration, sometimes lowering cost per invocation.. In practical terms, how memory allocation influences duration and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Lambda Right‑Sizing
Concept

Memory, CPU and Duration

Because CPU scales with memory in Lambda, increasing memory can speed execution and reduce billed duration. Test to find the cost‑effective memory allocation.

Example comparison
Function A: memory=512 MB, duration=300 ms
Function B: memory=1024 MB, duration=120 ms
Compare cost per invocation using duration × memory.
Concrete scenario
A parsing function spends CPU time on decoding. Doubling memory may halve duration. Measure invocations and duration before and after to choose the cheaper configuration per invocation.
Common mistake
Assuming lower memory always costs less. In Lambda, higher memory can reduce duration sufficiently to lower cost per call.
Key Takeaway

Treat Lambda sizing as an experiment: measure Duration and cost at multiple memory sizes to find the optimal point.

screens.title: Cost Optimization for Containers (ECS & EKS)
screens.narratorSegment: Containerized workloads require thoughtful resource allocation to avoid waste. In ECS task definitions and Kubernetes pod specs on EKS, you must set C P U and memory requests and limits. Requests tell the scheduler how much to reserve, and limits cap usage. Underestimating requests leads to poor placement or evictions; overestimating requests leads to poor packing and higher billable capacity. For ECS, using the EC2 launch type means you pay for the underlying instances; efficient packing reduces the number of instances required. Fargate bills per task, so it can be cost‑effective for bursty or unpredictable workloads because you avoid paying for idle nodes. In EKS, define requests and limits to help the scheduler pack pods tightly and avoid node overprovisioning. Regularly review node utilization and consider using smaller instance types or autoscaling to adjust capacity. The practical rule: set realistic requests based on metrics, set reasonable limits to protect neighbors, and choose Fargate when you want to avoid node management for variable workloads. Cost Optimization for Containers (ECS & EKS) means use requests and limits to enable efficient scheduler packing; choose fargate when avoiding idle node costs makes sense.. In practical terms, requests, limits, fargate vs ec2 launch types, and node utilization. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Containers
Architecture Guidance

Requests, limits and launch types

Set requests to indicate the resources your container needs and limits to prevent runaway consumption. Use smaller requests based on observed metrics and set limits to protect the cluster.

ECS (EC2)
Efficient packing reduces EC2 instance count. Monitor container instances for unused capacity and scale down nodes when safe.
Fargate
Pay per task; good for bursty workloads where node management would leave idle capacity otherwise.
EKS
Define pod requests and limits so the scheduler places pods efficiently. Adjust node sizes and autoscaling to match real demand.
Example
A web service with unpredictable traffic moved to Fargate for cost efficiency because it avoided paying for idle EC2 instances during quiet hours.
Pro Tip
Collect container metrics and tune requests from real data. Small, frequent adjustments keep packing optimal without harming reliability.
Key Takeaway

Correctly set requests and limits to improve packing and reduce node count; prefer Fargate when you want to avoid idle node costs for variable workloads.

Once you know where spend occurs, create a Budget scoped to those compute services. Set an alert threshold, for example 80 percent of your budgeted monthly amount, so you receive timely notifications. The chapter walks through creating a recurring monthly cost budget named Compute‑Service‑Budget and adding an 80 percent actual alert. This workflow prevents bill shock and turns cost monitoring into operational practice. A common governance mistake is relying only on monthly invoices; instead, configure ongoing reports and alerts so engineers can take corrective actions. Finally, couple budgets with tagging so you can alert on project or owner spend and assign accountability for corrective steps. Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Cost Explorer & Budgets
Workflow
  1. Open Cost Explorer and filter by compute services to identify top spenders.
  2. Group by Usage Type to find the specific resources driving cost.
  3. Create a monthly Cost Budget scoped to those services and add an 80% alert threshold.
  4. Apply tags to associate costs to owners and projects and tune Budgets accordingly.
Console example (illustrative)
Filter: Service = EC2 Instances, EC2 - Other, AWS Lambda, Amazon ECS, Fargate Group by: Usage Type Save report: Monthly costs by compute
Common mistake
Waiting for the monthly bill to take action. Budgets and alerts allow you to act before costs escalate.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Tagging Strategy for Cost Allocation
screens.narratorSegment: Tags are metadata key‑value pairs you apply to AWS resources to add context such as Project, Owner, Environment or CostCenter. They are crucial for cost allocation because Cost Explorer and Budgets can filter and group costs by tags. A consistent tagging strategy enables engineering teams and finance to run reports, apply chargebacks, and assign responsibility for high spend. When creating a tagging scheme, choose a small set of required keys that are meaningful across your organization and document allowed values. Also implement automation to enforce tags at creation time where possible and add periodic checks to catch untagged resources. A common governance mistake is having inconsistent tag names or optional tags that aren't consistently applied; this reduces the usefulness of reports. Finally, tag compute resources early — when instances, tasks or functions are provisioned — and ensure billing reports align to these tags for accurate allocation. Good tags make it easy to ask who owns the cost and why it exists. screens.title: Resource Lifecycle Management
screens.narratorSegment: Resource lifecycle management prevents waste by ensuring resources are created, used and terminated appropriately. Common sources of waste include idle EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes, and old AMIs or container images. Start by inventorying resources and identifying low‑utilization instances and unattached volumes. Implement automation like an EC2 Instance Scheduler to stop non‑business hours instances and scripts or policies to delete unattached EBS volumes and old AMIs after a retention period. For repositories and buckets, enforce lifecycle rules to remove or archive old artifacts. Maintain a tagging policy so resource owners can be notified and given the chance to justify retention. The chapter emphasizes automating cleanup wherever safe, because manual surveys are brittle. A critical practice is to include safe guards: require approval before deleting resources used in production and retain backups where necessary. The point is to make lifecycle management routine and auditable so waste is removed without risking critical data or uptime. Resource Lifecycle Management means automate stopping and cleanup of unused compute and storage resources while retaining safety checks and owner approvals for production assets.. In practical terms, identify and remove idle resources: instances, volumes, amis and repositories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common Mistakes & How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes repeatedly increase compute spend unnecessarily. First, leaving predictable, long‑running workloads on On‑Demand pricing wastes potential savings; the fix is to analyze historical usage and commit with Reserved Instances or Savings Plans. Second, resizing purely on average C P U without considering memory, input and output or traffic spikes causes performance regressions; the fix is to examine multiple metrics and validate with canary tests. Third, neglecting tags prevents accurate cost allocation and hampers chargeback; enforce a small set of required tags and automate validation. Fourth, failing to clean up unattached volumes or old images leads to silent charges; schedule automated cleanup with safe retention policies. Fifth, misconfiguring container requests and limits causes poor packing or evictions; set realistic requests based on observed container metrics. For each mistake, the defensive action is measurement first, testing second, and automation third. Make these three steps part of your operational checklist so you avoid repeating these common errors in production environments. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to make compute choices that reduce cost without hurting performance. We start by clarifying EC2 purchasing options — On‑Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans and Spot — and when each fits typical workloads. You will also learn right‑sizing techniques for EC2 and Lambda, how container resource requests and limits affect packing and billing for ECS and EKS, and why tagging plus lifecycle automation are essential for governance. I’ll give concrete examples you can use today: recognizing steady 24/7 services that suit Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, tuning Lambda memory to reduce duration, and cleaning up unattached volumes to stop unnecessary charges. Throughout, pay attention to three linked practices: monitor usage, choose the right purchase model, and automate lifecycle actions. These three reduce waste most reliably. By the end you’ll have a checklist to evaluate compute architecture decisions and a clear set of next steps to apply in your environment. Consider one workload you manage: which of these approaches would cut the most cost without adding risk?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to select the appropriate EC2 purchasing option for different workload patterns, from bursty test servers to steady 24/7 services. You will also be able to right‑size both EC2 instances and Lambda functions using utilization metrics and recommendations, improving performance and lowering cost. Additionally, you will understand how to configure container resource requests and limits so ECS and EKS schedules efficiently and avoids costly overprovisioning. Finally, you will apply cost management practices — Cost Explorer, Budgets, tagging, and resource lifecycle automation — to monitor, allocate, and remove wasteful resources. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can measure progress. For example, the ability to map a predictable 24/7 workload to a Reserved Instance or Savings Plan is a concrete milestone; so is creating a budget with an 80 percent alert threshold. These skills make your designs both cost‑aware and operationally sustainable.

In this second objectives slide we focus on applied skills you can practice immediately. You will learn to interpret CloudWatch metrics — C P U, memory, disk and network patterns — and translate them into right‑sizing actions. For Lambda, you will learn the relationship between memory allocation and execution duration so you can experiment and find a cost‑effective memory setting. For containers, you will practice setting requests and limits so schedulers pack workloads efficiently and prevent noisy neighbors. Finally, you will implement tagging conventions such as Project, Owner and Environment, and create an AWS Budget scoped to compute services with an 80 percent alert threshold. These are practical exercises: for example, set a budget named Compute‑Service‑Budget, scope it to EC2 and Lambda, and add an 80 percent email alert. Being able to do these steps ensures your architectures are cost‑aware from design through operation.

EC2 purchasing options determine how you pay for compute and directly affect cost at scale. On‑Demand instances are the most flexible: they let you start and stop instances with no long‑term commitment, but they are the most expensive per hour. Reserved Instances provide significant discounts for predictable, steady workloads when you commit for one or three years. The chapter notes discounts up to about seventy‑five percent for RIs when combined with the right payment options; they are best for services that run continuously and have consistent sizing. Savings Plans achieve similar or better savings with more flexibility: by committing to a sustained hourly spend for one or three years, you receive discounts that apply across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda — making them suitable for dynamic environments where instance types change. Spot Instances are the low‑cost option for fault‑tolerant, interruptible workloads; they can offer very deep discounts but require architectures that handle interruption. A common mistake is leaving predictable, steady workloads on On‑Demand. In practice, analyze historical utilization, then choose RIs or Savings Plans for steady baselines and Spot for flexible, batch or fault‑tolerant tasks. The core takeaway: match predictability to commitment for maximal savings.

Reserved Instances and Savings Plans both reduce cost for predictable compute, but they differ in flexibility and scope. Reserved Instances tie discounts to a specific instance family, region and tenancy when using Standard RIs; Convertible RIs allow some instance family changes but require compatible choices. The chapter highlights that RIs are ideal when you have stable, continuous workloads that will run on the same instance family for the commitment term. Savings Plans, by contrast, grant discounts based on a committed hourly spend and apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda. This makes Savings Plans especially useful in modern, dynamic environments where workloads may migrate from EC2 to Fargate or change instance families over time. A common decision pattern is to buy Savings Plans for broad baseline spend and use RIs only when you need instance‑level guarantees. Payment options and term length matter too: one‑year versus three‑year commitments and All Upfront payments affect the effective discount. The practical rule: if you need maximum flexibility across compute types, prefer Savings Plans; if you need instance‑specific pricing and you can commit to the same family, RIs may be slightly better in narrow cases.

Right‑sizing EC2 is a process, not a one‑time task. Start by collecting utilization metrics: C P U, memory, network input and output and disk input and output. Use CloudWatch to gather a historical view over several weeks or months, because short spikes can mislead decisions. Feed that usage history into AWS Compute Optimizer when available; it analyzes past behavior and recommends instance sizes, families and EBS volume adjustments. After you have recommendations, test changes with a canary or staging environment and monitor latency, error rates and user experience. If performance holds, plan a rollout and consider RIs or Savings Plans to cover the new, lower baseline. Always avoid two mistakes: downsizing purely on average C P U while ignoring spikes that need burst capacity, and changing sizes without validating real‑world performance. To iterate effectively, keep a rollback plan and tag instances with owner and purpose so you can track impact. The goal is to deliver the same or better performance with less billable capacity. Over time this process should be periodic and data‑driven, not reactive. Right‑Sizing EC2 Instances means measure, analyze with compute optimizer, test changes, validate performance, then commit and monitor to prevent regressions.. In practical terms, a practical workflow to identify and correct over‑provisioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lambda pricing depends on memory allocation and execution duration. Increasing memory increases C P U proportionally in Lambda, so some functions complete faster when given more memory. That faster completion can lower overall billed duration and therefore cost, despite the higher per‑millisecond memory price. Right‑sizing a function is an experiment: measure current Duration and Invocations in CloudWatch, try a higher memory configuration, and compare cost per invocation. The chapter recommends using the Duration metric to find the sweet spot. A concrete example: if a function at 512 MB runs in 300 milliseconds, and at 1024 MB it runs in 120 milliseconds, the second configuration can be cheaper per invocation even though memory doubled. A common misconception is that higher memory always costs more; in Lambda, C P U scaling can reduce duration enough to lower cost. The practical workflow is to test multiple memory sizes, record Duration and cost, and choose the memory setting that minimizes cost while meeting latency requirements. Right‑Sizing AWS Lambda means test memory sizes because more memory increases cpu and can reduce duration, sometimes lowering cost per invocation.. In practical terms, how memory allocation influences duration and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Containerized workloads require thoughtful resource allocation to avoid waste. In ECS task definitions and Kubernetes pod specs on EKS, you must set C P U and memory requests and limits. Requests tell the scheduler how much to reserve, and limits cap usage. Underestimating requests leads to poor placement or evictions; overestimating requests leads to poor packing and higher billable capacity. For ECS, using the EC2 launch type means you pay for the underlying instances; efficient packing reduces the number of instances required. Fargate bills per task, so it can be cost‑effective for bursty or unpredictable workloads because you avoid paying for idle nodes. Tags are metadata key‑value pairs you apply to AWS resources to add context such as Project, Owner, Environment or CostCenter. They are crucial for cost allocation because Cost Explorer and Budgets can filter and group costs by tags. A consistent tagging strategy enables engineering teams and finance to run reports, apply chargebacks, and assign responsibility for high spend. When creating a tagging scheme, choose a small set of required keys that are meaningful across your organization and document allowed values. Also implement automation to enforce tags at creation time where possible and add periodic checks to catch untagged resources. A common governance mistake is having inconsistent tag names or optional tags that aren't consistently applied; this reduces the usefulness of reports. Resource lifecycle management prevents waste by ensuring resources are created, used and terminated appropriately. Common sources of waste include idle EC2 instances, unattached EBS volumes, and old AMIs or container images. Start by inventorying resources and identifying low‑utilization instances and unattached volumes. Implement automation like an EC2 Instance Scheduler to stop non‑business hours instances and scripts or policies to delete unattached EBS volumes and old AMIs after a retention period. For repositories and buckets, enforce lifecycle rules to remove or archive old artifacts. Maintain a tagging policy so resource owners can be notified and given the chance to justify retention. The chapter emphasizes automating cleanup wherever safe, because manual surveys are brittle. A critical practice is to include safe guards: require approval before deleting resources used in production and retain backups where necessary. The point is to make lifecycle management routine and auditable so waste is removed without risking critical data or uptime. Several common mistakes repeatedly increase compute spend unnecessarily. First, leaving predictable, long‑running workloads on On‑Demand pricing wastes potential savings; the fix is to analyze historical usage and commit with Reserved Instances or Savings Plans. Second, resizing purely on average C P U without considering memory, input and output or traffic spikes causes performance regressions; the fix is to examine multiple metrics and validate with canary tests. Third, neglecting tags prevents accurate cost allocation and hampers chargeback; enforce a small set of required tags and automate validation. Fourth, failing to clean up unattached volumes or old images leads to silent charges; schedule automated cleanup with safe retention policies. Fifth, misconfiguring container requests and limits causes poor packing or evictions; set realistic requests based on observed container metrics. For each mistake, the defensive action is measurement first, testing second, and automation third. Make these three steps part of your operational checklist so you avoid repeating these common errors in production environments. An assessment helps cement the decision process for selecting purchase models. Imagine an internal analytics application running 24/7 with highly predictable usage for three years. The best choices are either Reserved Instances with a long commitment or a Compute Savings Plan. Reserved Instances can be purchased with All Upfront payment or other payment options; All Upfront usually yields the largest discount if you can provide capital. A Compute Savings Plan for three years can be preferable when you want flexibility across EC2, Fargate and Lambda. The assessment goal is to justify the choice by referencing predictability, term length, and flexibility needs. In a different scenario, for ephemeral batch jobs that tolerate interruptions, Spot Instances offer the largest savings.
